name: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
title: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
answer: Weighing the scientific consensus means assessing how much agreement exists across a body of research on a specific question. In literature review and evidence synthesis, this involves distinguishing findings that are repeatedly supported from those that remain contested or isolated. The work draws on a site library of 135 research papers and 10,555 extracted claims, which provides a structured base for comparing statements across studies. It is a descriptive practice, not a source of legal, financial, investment or medical advice.

sections.body: Weighing the scientific consensus means assessing how much agreement exists across a body of research on a specific question. In literature review and evidence synthesis, this involves distinguishing findings that are repeatedly supported from those that remain contested or isolated. The work draws on a site library of 135 research papers and 10,555 extracted claims, which provides a structured base for comparing statements across studies. It is a descriptive practice, not a source of legal, financial, investment or medical advice.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The process runs on indexed research corpora, structured claim databases, and tools for retrieving and comparing text across papers. Citation graphs and reference lists help trace how a finding has been treated by later work. Search and similarity functions allow an analyst to group claims that address the same question even when wording differs. No single model or tool is required; the infrastructure is a combination of a curated library, extracted claims, and standard text retrieval methods.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Analysts first define the review question and identify relevant studies through systematic search. Claims are then extracted from each paper and grouped by topic, often using the site's 10,555 extracted claims as a working set. Agreement is assessed by counting and weighting supporting, contradicting, and neutral statements, with attention to study design, sample size, and replication status. The result is a graded picture of consensus, from strong agreement to genuine dispute, rather than a simple vote count.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance is central: content on this site never links to the Consensus search tool; it links to the original paper, so every claim can be traced to its source. Risks include publication bias, selective citation, and the chance that a vocal minority of studies is mistaken for a consensus. Reviewers therefore document inclusion criteria, search dates, and how conflicting evidence was handled. The practice describes the state of evidence and does not tell a reader what decision to make.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward living evidence syntheses that update as new studies and claims are added to the library. Better extraction and grouping of claims may reduce the manual effort of comparing hundreds of papers. Future work is likely to attach explicit confidence or uncertainty scores to consensus statements, and to link those scores to the underlying study quality and replication record. The goal is a more current and transparent map of where scientific agreement actually stands.
